title: What Is AI, Really? — Module Quiz

items.q: Your bank flags a card payment as 'unusual' for human review. In this course's terms, the AI is:
options: Suggesting — a person or process still decides
items.explain: Most everyday AI flags and suggests; accountability for the decision stays with people and processes.

items.q: The key difference between rule-based systems and machine learning is:
options: Rules are written by people; ML patterns are learned from examples
items.explain: Expert systems encoded human-written rules; ML flipped to learning patterns from labelled examples.

options: Promises outran what brittle systems could deliver, and funding collapsed
Researchers solved AI and moved on
items.explain: Twice, inflated expectations met narrow, brittle capability — a calibration lesson for reading today's headlines too.

items.q: A hiring model trained mostly on one demographic's successful applications will most likely:
options: Reproduce the skew — biased examples produce biased predictions
items.explain: Models mirror their training data. Incomplete or skewed examples become skewed patterns — the mechanism behind most AI bias stories.

options: The weights — millions of small dials nudged after each example
items.explain: Learning is dial-turning: each example nudges weights so correct outputs become slightly more likely.

options: It labels inputs from a fixed list
It produces new content, one predicted piece at a time
It stores more data than other systems
items.explain: Recognisers output labels; generators produce new text, images, or audio via repeated next-piece prediction.

items.q: An LLM 'remembers' something from earlier in your chat because:
options: It has a permanent memory of you
That text is still inside its context window, which it re-reads each prediction
It looked the chat up in a database
items.explain: The context window is working memory: inside it, text influences answers; outside it, text doesn't exist for the model.

options: Specific numbers, names, citations, and recent events
items.explain: Where training patterns are thin — specifics, niches, recency — plausible generation fills gaps with confident inventions.

items.q: Asking a model 'are you sure?' after a doubtful claim mainly produces:
options: More plausible-sounding text — confidence was never connected to accuracy
items.explain: Fluency is constant, accuracy variable. Verification lives outside the model: sources, documents, your three-question habit.

items.q: Per the capability map, the safest home turf for today's AI is:
options: Language and pattern work you can check, on material you provide
items.explain: Strong zone = verifiable transformation of supplied material; weak zone = unverifiable specifics and accountable human judgement.

items.q: The 'golden rule' closing module E1 is:
options: Use AI where you can verify; keep a human in the loop where errors cost
items.explain: Stakes determine verification. This sentence underwrites every workflow in the rest of the course.

items.q: A model confidently rejects a ripe green-skinned mango variety it never saw in training. This illustrates:
options: Patterns only cover what examples covered — confidence reflects match strength, not truth
items.explain: Unfamiliar inputs meet confident pattern-matching. The fruit-stall analogy scales to every AI failure you'll read about.
